title: After-action: memory + NIC throttling latency blip
content:
Summary:

On 2026-02-24 (UTC) at ~15:07 we observed a 3.2x p99 latency spike for the hosted generation endpoint (v1/generate) affecting a small cohort of customers for ~14 minutes. Error rates did not increase materially; errors were <0.2%, but tail latency violations caused SLO alerts and customer-facing degradations for streaming responses.

Impact:
- Scope: ~7% of production traffic routed to cluster-us-west-2 (multi-tenant pool).
- Customer-visible: increased streaming chunk delays (clients saw pauses of ~600–800ms between stream chunks).
- SLO: 99th percentile latency exceeded target for ~14 minutes triggering pager.
- No data loss, no model correctness regressions.

Detection and Triage Timeline (high level):
- 15:07: Alert: p99 latency > SLO threshold for hosted-generate-us-west-2-route.
- 15:09: On-call (Luca) confirmed via Console traces that tail spikes were concentrated on a subset of nodes and that CPU/GPU utilization looked normal.
- 15:12: Initial flamegraphs from perf showed long stacks in the kernel TCP transmit path and in user-space around TLS_sendmsg.
- 15:18: eBPF tcpconnect/tcptracer showed elevated syscall latency for sendmsg and epoll_wait on affected processes.
- 15:25: Team hypothesis formed: intermittent NIC/driver offload regression causing segmentation/serialization stalls for small TLS-record writes combined with momentary high malloc contention in our custom arena when many streaming requests started simultaneously.
- 15:30: Mitigation 1 (quick rollback): disable NIC offloading flags on affected nodes via remote script; immediate reduction in syscall latencies observed.
- 15:40: Mitigation 2 (hotfix): hotpatch to allocator configuration (temporarily increase per-thread cache and preallocate small buffers for streaming path).
- 15:55: Metrics returned near baseline; alert resolved at 15:58 after two stabilization windows.

What we measured / profiling notes:
- Workloads: streaming generation with many small chunks (typical to chat UI).
- Tools used: perf, eBPF (bcc+tpc), strace on sampled processes, kernel dmesg, NIC stats (ethtool), tcpdump for packet pacing analysis.
- Observations:
  - sendmsg syscall latency distribution showed heavy tail aligning with p99+ events; samples pointed into kernel's TCP transmit path and skb queues.
  - ethtool showed offload counters incrementing anomalies (TSO/GSO path).
  - dmesg contained driver-level warnings about transmit completions timing out (rare, but aligned with timestamps).
  - User-space memory profiler (heap-prof) showed spikes in small-object allocations/classes used by streaming encoder path; contention in jemalloc arenas was visible under high fan-in.
  - No GPU stalls or deep kernel preemption events were correlated.

Root cause hypothesis (final):
A combination of factors created a transient amplification of tail latency: 
1) A recent kernel+NIC driver micro-update (rolled to a subset of hosts by infra change 2026-02-23) introduced a regression in the offload completion path causing occasional long transmit completion waits for small TLS-framed writes. The offload bug manifested under high concurrent small-packet workloads (like streaming).
2) Simultaneously, our streaming path had a small-allocation hot path that, under sudden fan-in, used the default jemalloc arena settings; on some hosts this produced malloc locking contention and brief stalls that serialized write threads, increasing the probability that the driver bug hit during those windows.
3) The combined effect was a higher chance of transient syscall serialization around sendmsg/epoll_wait, producing observed chunk pauses. Each factor alone would likely not breach SLO; combined they produced the incident.

Immediate mitigations performed and rationale:
- Disabled NIC offloads (TSO/GSO) on affected nodes (rollback of driver behavior) -> removed the offload completion path so kernel transmitted inline, eliminating the driver-completion stalls. Quick and reversible. (Applied 15:30)
- Allocator hotfix: increased per-thread caches and added a small buffer pool for streaming write buffers (hotpatch, safe change) to reduce small-allocation contention during peaks. (Applied 15:40)
- Traffic steering: temporarily shifted a portion of traffic to a different pool without the recent kernel roll (fallback pool) during validation window.

Hotfix validation and testing:
- Canary run: deployed allocator hotfix to 5 canary nodes in us-west-2 under 2x traffic replay of streaming workload for 30 minutes. Observed p99 within 110% of baseline and no sendmsg tails.
- Stress tests: synthetic test that mimicked chat UI with 1000 concurrent streams with small chunks confirmed mitigations reduced allocation stalls by ~86% and removed sendmsg tail events.
- Postmortem verification: after rolling out mitigations to the rest of the cluster, we ran a 2-hour steady-state replay and verified SLO compliance and no driver dmesg warnings.

Longer-term fixes and action items (owners & ETA):
- INFRA-1471 (owner: Samir Patel, ETA 2026-03-12): Fully roll back the kernel+driver micro-update across clusters until vendor patch is available or prove stable with extended soak.
- RUNTIME-983 (owner: Maya Chen, ETA 2026-04-02): Replace the temporary allocator hotpatch with a permanent streaming buffer pool implementation (lock-free freelist) and add per-node telemetry for allocation contention.
- OBS-760 (owner: Hannah Lee, ETA 2026-03-20): Add eBPF-based automated detection that monitors sendmsg/syscall tail distributions and driver offload anomaly counters to produce early warning.
- QA-441 (owner: Priya Nair, ETA 2026-03-08): Add a synthetic streaming tail-latency test to nightly regression that specifically exercises small-chunk TLS streaming with realistic interleaving.
- DOCS-120 (owner: Luca Romano, ETA 2026-03-01): Runbook update: include NIC-driver-offload toggles and allocator rollback steps with one-command playbooks.

Risks and follow-ups:
- Vendor driver patch timeline uncertain; INFRA must coordinate with cloud provider and NIC vendor. If vendor fix delays, disabling offload permanently has cost/CPU tradeoffs; quantify CPU delta and update cost model.
- The temporary allocator change reduces latency but increases memory headroom usage by ~4% on canary; monitor OOM patterns.
- Need to confirm no regression on Dedicated clusters where pinned hardware/driver versions may differ.

Appendix (notes from incident runbook & raw traces):
- Key artifacts:
  - JIRA INC ticket: JIRA-INC-3521 (incident tracking)
  - Hotfix PR: GH-PR-4812 (allocator buffer pool quickpatch)
  - Slack thread: https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C03KJS9F/thread-1612
  - Example perf sample (snippet): system call busy in tcp_transmit_skb -> __tcp_transmit_skb -> napi_gro_receive -> nic_xmit_complete (timestamps aligned with driver warnings).

Conclusions:
This incident was not a single-point software bug in the serving runtime but an emergent interaction between a vendor driver regression and a user-space allocation pattern that created serialization windows. Our remediation path prioritized reversible infra changes (disable offload) and a low-risk user-space patch to prevent re-occurrence. The recommended long-term path is (1) permanent allocator redesign for streaming, (2) improved telemetry/early detection for syscall tail anomaly, and (3) coordination with infra/vendor for driver stability testing before kernel/driver rollouts.

If you have comments or additional data to add (heap profiles, full perf captures), please append to the linked Slack thread or the JIRA ticket.

Document owner: Maya Chen (eng-serving-runtime)
